posts.title: How SEWA's Uncertainty Engine quantifies what it does not know
posts.subtitle: Most clinical AI gives a single confidence score. SEWA tells you when it is uncertain.
posts.excerpt: In clinical AI, a confidence score without uncertainty quantification is incomplete. A model that is 60% confident is not 60% certain — it may be guessing. SEWA's Uncertainty Engine decomposes predictive uncertainty into aleatoric and epistatic components, surfacing cases where the model's knowledge is thin so they receive deeper review.
posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo

posts.title: Metacognition in clinical AI: how SEWA catches its own hallucinations
posts.subtitle: Large language models hallucinate — and so can clinical AI. The Metacognition Engine intercepts them before they reach a clinician.
posts.excerpt: When an AI system confidently states a finding that is not present, that is a hallucination. In radiology, a hallucinated pulmonary embolism triggers an unnecessary CT pulmonary angiogram; a missed pneumothorax delays treatment. SEWA's Metacognition Engine catches 96.3% of hallucinations in internal testing, acting as a pre-dispatch gate that checks every output against anatomical and physiological constraints before it is ever shown to a clinician.
posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo

posts.title: The SEWA safety architecture: uncertainty decomposition, hallucination gate, and non-bypassable sign-off
posts.subtitle: Three layers, each addressing a distinct failure mode, working together to keep patients safe
posts.excerpt: SEWA's safety architecture is built from three stacked layers, each addressing a different way clinical AI can fail. The Uncertainty Engine quantifies what the model knows and does not know. The Metacognition Gate checks for hallucinations and physiologically impossible outputs. And the database-layer sign-off enforces mandatory human review that cannot be bypassed, archived, or overridden — ensuring that no automated finding reaches a patient's care pathway without a clinician's explicit decision.
posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo

posts.title: Edge-first clinical AI: how SEWA runs offline on low-RAM devices and syncs when connectivity resumes
posts.subtitle: 70% of African hospitals cannot rely on consistent internet. SEWA was built to work regardless.
posts.excerpt: SEWA's edge deployment runs on under 20 MB of RAM using INT8-quantised models, operates completely offline, and syncs to the cloud only when connectivity resumes. The Go DICOM service ingests scans locally, runs inference on-device, stores encrypted results, and queues uploads automatically. For NHS Trusts with resilient networks and for hospitals in low-connectivity settings alike, the architecture delivers the same safety guarantees — uncertainty decomposition, hallucination gating, and non-bypassable sign-off — whether online or not.
posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo

posts.title: Non-bypassable human sign-off: why SEWA enforces radiologist review at the database layer
posts.subtitle: UI-level review can be skipped. Database-layer sign-off cannot.
posts.excerpt: Most clinical AI platforms place human review at the user interface level — a prompt the radiologist can dismiss, a modal they can close, a workflow they can override. SEWA enforces sign-off at the database layer: a finding is never persisted as an approved result unless a consultant radiologist has explicitly accepted it. There is no UI toggle, no administrator override, and no bypass path. The architecture makes human oversight a structural requirement, not a convenience setting.
posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo

posts.title: Uncertainty quantification in medical AI: why a single confidence score is not enough
posts.subtitle: What aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty mean for patient safety — and why the industry is only beginning to adopt them
posts.excerpt: Nearly every clinical AI platform reports a confidence or accuracy metric. Few tell you when their model is uncertain. This matters because uncertainty is not a flaw — it is information. A model that says 'I am 55% confident' is fundamentally different from one that says 'I am 99% confident' — yet both are often presented identically. Understanding uncertainty quantification is the first step toward trusting clinical AI safely.
posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo

posts.title: Why hallucination gates matter in clinical AI — and what happens without one
posts.subtitle: Hallucinations are not a language-model problem alone. They are a patient-safety problem.
posts.excerpt: When a large language model invents a citation, the harm is reputational. When a clinical AI hallucinates a pulmonary embolism on a normal chest X-ray, the harm is a patient undergoing an unnecessary invasive procedure — or a radiologist losing trust in the entire category of AI assistance. A pre-dispatch hallucination gate intercepts these outputs before they reach a clinician, checking every finding against anatomical, physiological, and contextual constraints.

posts.title: What is a trust architecture in clinical AI? The framework the market is missing
posts.subtitle: Uncertainty decomposition, hallucination gating, non-bypassable sign-off, and offline continuity — why none of these exist together in a single platform yet

posts.title: MHRA reforms and the UKCA pathway: where SEWA sits on the regulatory trajectory
posts.subtitle: The 22 July 2025 international-reliance package and the UKCA Class IIb route — what it means for clinical AI
posts.excerpt: MHRA's 22 July 2025 reform package introduced international reliance provisions and a streamlined UKCA marking route for innovative medical devices, including AI-based SaMD. For SEWA, the trajectory is clear: shadow trial (prospective, 6-month, primary endpoint door-to-alert under 5 minutes) → NIHR EME → UKCA Class IIb (Q2 2027). This post maps the regulatory journey and explains what each milestone requires.
posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo

posts.title: DCB0129, DCB0160 and NHS AI procurement: what every clinical AI vendor must demonstrate
posts.subtitle: The DSPT, DTAC, and AI Diagnostic Fund are reshaping how the NHS evaluates and funds AI — SEWA is built for every checkpoint
posts.excerpt: NHS Digital Security and Trust (DCB0129) and the Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DCB0160) set the governance bar for any AI deployed in NHS England. Combined with the AI Diagnostic Fund and the Digital Technologies Assessment Checklist (DTAC), these frameworks define what procurement teams must see before adoption. SEWA's documentation pack addresses each checkpoint directly — from cyber-resilience to data governance to clinical safety evidence.
posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo

posts.title: The evidence bar in clinical AI: what Brainomix's Lancet study and DeepHealth's GEMINI study set
posts.subtitle: The market's winners won on breadth, workflow, or evidence — and the bar for the next entrant just got higher
posts.excerpt: Clinical AI adoption in the NHS still stalls on alert fatigue, opaque single scores, bypassable oversight, cloud-only outages, and thin real-world evidence. Brainomix's Lancet Digital Health study (452,952 patients, 107 NHS hospitals) and DeepHealth/Kheiron's GEMINI study (10,889 women) show what the evidence bar now looks like. These are the templates any platform must meet to convert a strong architecture into regulated, evidenced, deployed reality.
posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo

posts.title: The trustworthy-AI shortage: why the market has an AI problem that is not about supply
posts.subtitle: The NHS does not have an AI shortage — it has a trustworthy AI shortage
posts.excerpt: Clinical imaging AI is crowded with well-funded detection tools — yet none has publicly delivered a full trust architecture. The NHS already uses AI at scale (at least 54% of radiology departments, RCR 2023) and funds it (£123M AI in Health and Care Award, AI Diagnostic Fund), but adoption still stalls on alert fatigue, opaque single scores, bypassable oversight, cloud-only outages, and thin real-world evidence. The market does not need another detection tool. It needs trustworthy AI.
posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo

posts.title: The evidence pathway: from shadow trial to NIHR EME to UKCA Class IIb
posts.subtitle: A transparent roadmap for converting an architecturally differentiated platform into regulated, evidenced, deployed reality
posts.excerpt: SEWA's challenge is not identity — it is proof. The roadmap is deliberate: a prospective shadow trial (6 months, primary endpoint door-to-alert under 5 minutes) feeds into an NIHR EME application, which in turn supports a UKCA Class IIb submission (Q2 2027). Each phase is designed to build the independent clinical validation that the market demands, following the evidence-bar templates set by Brainomix and DeepHealth.
posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo

posts.title: PPIE, the NIHR research programme, and how to join SEWA's clinical validation

The research programme, supported by the NIHR Research Delivery Network, includes patient advisory panels, NHS clinical leads across multiple regions, and a governance framework that meets NIHR expectations. This post explains how PPIE shapes the study design, how clinical sites are selected, and how partners and research sites can join.
posts.author: Dolapo Ariyo
